description: Material profiles. Every fact lists the exact source quotes behind it; scripts/verify_cards.py checks them against the NASA PDFs and PSI tables.

materials.name: SIBAL fabric
materials.data_status_text: Prediction model available: 47 measured microgravity tests with burn and no-burn outcomes (BASS, BASS-II and Saffire I-IV).
materials.summary: A custom woven fabric made for NASA's SIBAL project and later used as a fabric fuel in BASS, Saffire and FM2.

quotes.text: a composite fabric consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight).
The thickness of the sample is about 0.32 mm with an area density 18.2 mg/cm2.
The fabric is custom-made for a previous project SIBAL
where on Earth’s gravity it extinguishes immediately after ignition.

facts.label: In microgravity
facts.value: burned in gentle flow; quenched only at 1 to 5 cm/s

quotes.text: The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s)
SIBAL fabric has been found to only burn downward in air in lunar gravity

materials.name: PMMA (acrylic)
materials.data_status_text: Evidence only: 43 burn results from 20 flat-slab tests, all of which burned, so no burn boundary can be fitted. The rod boundary is reported against stretch rate, not airflow.
materials.summary: The clear plastic known as acrylic. NASA has burned it as slabs and rods on the ISS (BASS-II), in Saffire and in FM2 ground tests.

quotes.text: PMMA polymethylmethacrylate (acrylic)
the observed upward flame spread limit of 15.4 percent O2 (in normal gravity with an additional 4-cm/s forced flow (Ref. 23))
The minimum O2 concentration of 13.5 percent O2 at a of 8 to 12 s–1
A total of 20 PMMA flat samples were burnt during the BASS–II experimentation (Table 5.1).

facts.label: Exploration habitats
facts.value: an acrylic equipment case was judged unacceptable

quotes.text: The MinION has a clear PMMA (i.e., acrylic) case, which will not be acceptable for Exploration environments due to flammability concerns.

materials.name: Nomex
materials.data_status_text: Evidence only: 4 microgravity results from three different test setups, and the sources disagree, so no prediction is made.
materials.summary: A fire-retardant meta-aramid fabric commonly used on the ISS. It does not melt or drip, and its fibers swell to seal the weave when heated.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: meta-aramid fabric commonly used on the ISS

quotes.text: The material is a meta-aramid fabric commonly used on the ISS called Nomex® HT90-40.
Nomex HT90-40 is a 12 mil thick fire retarded aromatic nylon fabric which does not melt or drip as it burns.
On Earth, it will only burn if the oxygen concentration is increased to around 24 to 25%.

quotes.text: ULOI: 23.5% O2

facts.value: unlikely to meet requirements above 30% O2

quotes.text: Many ISS materials have been shown to meet flammability requirements at 10.2 psia and 30% O2, but are unlikely to meet the requirements at higher O2 concentrations.

materials.name: Silicone
materials.data_status_text: Evidence only: 4 Saffire-II samples, all of which barely burned in microgravity, so no burn boundary can be fitted.
materials.summary: Silicone rubber. In upward burning it deposits a silica layer on the fresh fuel that acts as a thermal barrier and can stop the flame spreading.

quotes.text: Silicone Rubber, R5789 21
quotes.context: Table 1: material, batch number, limiting oxygen index (%)

quotes.text: Data shown are lowest values listed in ASTM Manual 36, 2nd Edition, Table 3-12.

facts.label: On Earth (NASA Test 1)
facts.value: upward limit 19.7% (0.25 mm) to 23.4% O2 (1.00 mm)

quotes.text: The ULOI is the Upward Limiting Oxygen Index for which 50% of the repeat samples pass and 50% fail Test 1.
The increased flammability for downward spreading flames relative to upward ones is uncommon.

facts.label: Why
facts.value: a silica layer insulates the fresh fuel

quotes.text: The reason for the increased flammability in the downward direction compared to upward is attributed to the deposition of a silica layer onto the fresh fuel in the upward case.
It has been shown that this layer acts as a thermal barrier, which prohibits the fuel from reaching the pyrolysis temperature fast enough to sustain flame spread.
